section.title: The Reign of the Righteous King
section.sectionRationale: The great royal psalm for Solomon, closing Book II with the note that 'the prayers of David son of Jesse are ended,' its vision of a universal, everlasting, poor-lifting reign so far exceeds any human king that it has always been read as reaching beyond Solomon to the Messiah, the true King.
section.thesis: Prayed over Solomon, this psalm's vision of a king who judges with righteousness, rescues the needy, and reigns from sea to sea until all nations are blessed in him finds its only adequate fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the true and everlasting King.
section.frameNote: Six movements: a prayer for a just king, verses 1 to 4; a reign marked by peace, verses 5 to 7; universal dominion, verses 8 to 11; compassion for the needy, verses 12 to 14; enduring blessing and fame, verses 15 to 17; closing doxology and the end of David's prayers, verses 18 to 20.

units.label: A prayer for a just king

verses.text: Of Solomon. Endow the king with Your {{mishpat|justice}}, O God, and the son of the king with Your righteousness.
May he judge Your people with righteousness and Your afflicted with justice.
May the mountains bring peace to the people, and the hills bring righteousness.
May he vindicate the afflicted among the people; may he save the children of the needy and crush the oppressor.

units.label: A reign marked by peace
units.note: as long as the sun shines

verses.text: May they fear him as long as the sun shines, as long as the moon remains, through all generations.
May he be like rain that falls on freshly cut grass, like spring showers that water the earth.
May the righteous flourish in his days and prosperity abound until the moon is no more.
May he rule from sea to sea, and from the Euphrates to the ends of the earth.
May the nomads bow before him, and his enemies lick the dust.
May the kings of Tarshish and distant shores bring tribute; may the kings of Sheba and Seba offer gifts.
May all kings bow down to him and all nations serve him.
For he will deliver the needy who cry out and the afflicted who have no helper.
He will take pity on the poor and needy and save the lives of the oppressed.
He will redeem them from oppression and violence, for their blood is precious in his sight.
Long may he live! May gold from Sheba be given him. May people ever pray for him; may they bless him all day long.
May there be an abundance of grain in the land; may it sway atop the hills. May its fruit trees flourish like the forests of Lebanon, the people of its cities like the grass of the field.
May his name endure forever; may his name continue as long as the sun shines. In him may all nations be {{barak|blessed}}; may they call him blessed.

units.label: Doxology and the end of David's prayers

verses.text: Blessed be the LORD God, the God of Israel, who alone does marvelous deeds.
And blessed be His glorious name forever; may all the earth be filled with His glory. Amen and amen.
Thus conclude the prayers of David son of Jesse.

mishpat.gloss: Justice, judgment, the exercise of fair rule. The psalm opens by asking God to give the king His own justice, not merely human fairness, so that the king's rule reflects God's own character.

barak.gloss: To bless, to kneel in homage. Verse 17's promise that 'all nations be blessed' in this king echoes the promise to Abraham, Genesis 12:3, tying the royal hope of this psalm to God's ancient covenant purpose for the whole world.

basic.context: Prayed 'of Solomon,' likely David's prayer for his son at the transfer of the crown, this psalm asks God to give the king His own justice and righteousness so that his reign brings peace, rescues the poor, and extends to the ends of the earth.
basic.hermeneutics: No earthly king, not even Solomon at his height, ever ruled with the perfection, universality, and endless duration this psalm describes. Ancient and Christian readers alike have taken this as evidence the psalm intentionally reaches past Solomon to the Messiah.
basic.originalLanguages: The king is asked to embody mishpat, justice, God's own standard of right rule, and the psalm's climax promises that in him all nations will be barak, blessed, deliberately echoing God's ancient promise to Abraham that all peoples would be blessed through his offspring.
basic.typology: The universal, everlasting, poor-defending king of this psalm is a type fulfilled in Jesus Christ, the true Son of David whose kingdom has no end, whose care for the needy exceeds any earthly ruler's, and in whom the Abrahamic blessing to all nations finally comes to pass.
basic.christ: Every feature of this ideal king, universal reign from sea to sea, everlasting name, compassion for the poor, blessing to all nations, is fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of David whose kingdom Luke 1:32-33 declares will never end and before whom Revelation 11:15 pictures every kingdom of the earth finally bowing.
basic.god: God is the source of the king's justice and righteousness; the king's rule is asked for, not assumed, showing that true and lasting authority to rule rightly comes from God alone.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 11:1-10 and Isaiah 9:6-7 describe the same righteous, peace-bringing king. Galatians 3:16 identifies Abraham's promised offspring, through whom all nations are blessed, as Christ. Revelation 11:15 proclaims the kingdoms of this world have become the kingdom of the Lord and of His Christ.
basic.oneStory: This prayer for Solomon's righteous, universal, poor-lifting reign was too large for Solomon or any human king to fulfill, and so it points forward through the whole story of Scripture to Jesus Christ, the true King in whom God's ancient promise that all nations would be blessed finally comes true.

context.literary:
Psalm 72 is one long sentence of wishes. Almost every line begins 'may he' or 'may they,' and the prayer runs in widening circles. It begins at the king's own person and court, verses 1 to 4, and then reaches out to the creation that answers his rule, verses 5 to 7, to the far nations, verses 8 to 11, and back to the poor whose cry he hears, verses 12 to 14. It ends with the prosperity and fame of his reign, verses 15 to 17, and a doxology, verses 18 and 19. The movement is from throne to earth to world and then to God.

Two words hold the opening together. 'Justice' and 'righteousness' appear in verse 1, are repeated in reverse in verse 2, and reappear in verse 3 as gifts the mountains and hills bring to the people. The king is not the source of them. They are given to him in verse 1, which is what the first line asks, and through him they flow out to the poor. The picture of the hills bringing righteousness is deliberate: justice is meant to be the climate of the land, not a rare event in a court.

The middle of the psalm is a matched pair. Verses 4 and 12 to 14 are about the poor, with the phrases 'afflicted,' 'needy' and 'oppressed' recurring in both, and they surround the long stretch in between about sun, moon, rain, sea and distant kings. The royal glory is bracketed by the poor. The reader is meant to feel that the empire is only worth having if it protects the weak.

Verses 5 and 17 form another frame: both speak of the sun and moon, the emblems of endurance, and of the king's name lasting 'as long as the sun shines.' The psalm makes the king's reign cosmic in duration, while the middle rains, harvests and crowded cities make it earthly in content. The final section pours it all into praise, and the psalm ends with a note that seals Book II.
context.historical:
The Hebrew title can mean 'of Solomon' or 'for Solomon,' and the tradition that David prayed it over his son is old. The narrative in 1 Kings 1 and 2 supplies the setting: David is old, the succession is disputed, and Solomon is anointed in the middle of a crisis. A prayer that the son of the king would be given God's own justice suits that moment. It also matches Solomon's first request at Gibeon, when he asked for an understanding heart to judge God's people, 1 Kings 3:9.

Solomon's name means 'peace,' and the promise to David was that his son would be a man of rest whose reign brings peace to Israel, 1 Chronicles 22:9. Psalm 72 asks that this be fulfilled. The Queen of Sheba, who came to test Solomon, said that God had made him king 'to carry out justice and righteousness,' 1 Kings 10:9, which is almost the language of the psalm's first verse. Solomon's reign did bring extraordinary peace and wealth, and the kingdoms from the Euphrates to Egypt paid tribute, 1 Kings 4:21.

Yet the psalm reaches beyond what the history could hold. Solomon's reign ended with a king whose foreign wives turned his heart from the LORD, 1 Kings 11:1 to 4, and the people begged his son to lighten the heavy yoke his father had put on them, 1 Kings 12:4. The poor whom the psalm had in view suffered under the king who was to protect them. Israel's own history is therefore the best commentary on the psalm's unfulfilled wishes.

The language is also that of ancient royal ideology. Kings across the ancient world were praised as defenders of the weak, as bringers of rain and fertility, as rulers to the ends of the earth. Israel adopted the form and reshaped it: the king's justice is a gift of God, the poor are the special charge of the king, and the rule is finally God's own. The psalm also carries Israel's covenant memory in verse 8, whose sea to sea and Euphrates recall the land promise made to Abraham, Genesis 15:18, and the promises to David's line, Psalm 89:27.
context.canonical:
The psalm's last verses form the closing seal of Book II, and the canon reads that seal in more than one way. 'Thus conclude the prayers of David son of Jesse,' verse 20, marks the end of a collection, although more psalms of David appear later in the Psalter. The note holds the psalm as the summit of David's prayers: the last thing he asked for was a king who would rule with God's justice.

Within the book of Psalms, Psalm 72 is answered by Psalm 89, which sits at the end of Book III. There the Davidic covenant appears to have failed, and the psalmist asks where God's promises to David have gone. The hopes of Psalm 72, an enduring name, a throne like the sun and moon, Psalm 89:36 and 37, are the same hopes, now tested by exile. The Psalter as a whole is the story of that promise tested and renewed.

The prophets take up the ideal directly. Isaiah promises a shoot from the stump of Jesse who will judge the poor with righteousness and decide with equity for the lowly, Isaiah 11:4. Isaiah 9:6 and 7 speaks of a child on David's throne with no end to the increase of his government and peace. Jeremiah promises a righteous Branch who will administer justice and righteousness, Jeremiah 23:5. Zechariah 9:9 and 10 has a king who rides on a donkey, brings peace to the nations, and whose dominion extends 'from sea to sea, and from the Euphrates to the ends of the earth,' words almost identical to Psalm 72:8. Isaiah 60:6 sees the caravans from Sheba bringing gold and frankincense, as Psalm 72:10 and 15 hoped.

The New Testament brings the pattern to Jesus. The magi come with gold, frankincense and myrrh, Matthew 2:11. Jesus says that the Queen of the South came to hear Solomon's wisdom, and now One greater than Solomon is here, Matthew 12:42. Gabriel tells Mary that her son will have David's throne and that His kingdom will never end, Luke 1:32 and 33. And Revelation announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, Revelation 11:15, while the kings of the earth bring their glory into the city, Revelation 21:24. Psalm 72 is one of the places where the canon most clearly leans toward a coming King.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalm's author wanted Israel to understand what a king is for. Its first line is not a request for military success or wealth. It asks for justice and righteousness, and it defines the king by his treatment of the poor. Any hearer, and above all any later prince, was meant to see that the standard of his reign was the condition of the weakest people in it: the afflicted, the needy, the children of the poor, those with no helper.

The author also meant to teach dependence. A king is given God's justice, verse 1. It does not come from his own wisdom or from the nation's institutions. This matters because Israel's kings were forever tempted to think that power made them right. The psalm opens with a prayer because the king's justice is a gift, and the people are asked to ask for it on his behalf.

Third, the author intended to place the king's reign inside the promise to Abraham. The last wish, 'In him may all nations be blessed,' verse 17, gives Israel's king a purpose beyond Israel. He is to be the means by which God fulfills the promise to bless the nations. A first hearer might have heard in that line a challenge to any narrowness of view: the throne exists for the blessing of the world.

The author leaves the reader with a doxology, so that the whole vast prayer ends not in the king but in the LORD, 'who alone does marvelous deeds,' verse 18. The king is a servant of a purpose bigger than himself, and the praise goes to the One who gives him what he needs.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm is a prayer, and its grammar is that of wishing. Everything it says about the king's reign is what the petitioners want, not a report of what happened. It does not claim that Solomon ruled so, and Israel's history shows he did not. Reading it as a description of Solomon's actual reign misses the sting it carries when set beside 1 Kings 11 and 12.

What it prescribes is a standard for all who hold authority. Rulers, judges, employers and anyone else with power over others are to judge the afflicted with justice, vindicate the poor, and treat the blood of the oppressed as precious, verse 14. The same demand appears in Psalm 82:3 and 4, Proverbs 29:14 and Proverbs 31:8 and 9. Christians in public life are meant to measure their work by the same standard.

The psalm also prescribes a habit of prayer for those in authority. It shows a people praying for their king, and Paul asks for the same in 1 Timothy 2:1 and 2. Believers do not merely evaluate governments; they intercede for them.

A caution comes with the sweeping language of dominion, verses 8 to 11. It should not be read as a charter for conquest or for Christian domination of the earth. The New Testament reads the enemies who lick the dust as a picture of the defeat of every power opposed to Christ, and the nations that bring their gifts as people gathered by the gospel, not by force.

debates.question: Is Psalm 72 a prayer for Solomon that was never fully realized, or a deliberately messianic psalm from the start?

views.label: A prayer for Solomon in the exalted style of royal psalms
views.case: The title names Solomon, and ancient Near Eastern royal poetry uses similar hyperbole for kings, so the language of endless rule and universal tribute need not point beyond the historical king.

views.label: A prayer written to exceed any human king
views.case: An everlasting name, dominion to the ends of the earth and the blessing of all nations go beyond what any monarch achieved, and Jewish and Christian tradition has long read the psalm as messianic.

debates.bearing: Whichever start one takes, Solomon's real but limited reign becomes a signpost, and the unfulfilled excess of the psalm drives the reader toward the greater King the New Testament identifies as Jesus.

debates.question: Are the verbs wishes or predictions?

views.label: Wishes and prayers
views.case: The Hebrew forms most naturally read as jussives here, 'may he,' and the psalm is introduced as a prayer and closed as one of the prayers of David. Most modern translations, including the BSB, follow this.

views.label: Predictions of what the king will do
views.case: Many older translations render the verbs as futures, 'he will judge,' and read the psalm as a prophecy. The switch to plain futures in verses 12 to 14 gives the reason: 'he will deliver the needy.'

debates.bearing: The two are close. A prayer that rests on God's promises is also an expression of confidence, and a psalm that predicts is also a psalm that asks. The BSB itself changes to 'he will' in verses 12 to 14, as though wish becomes assurance.

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm's first verse pairs mishpat, justice, with tsedaqah, righteousness, and the two words come back throughout. Mishpat is right decision, the verdict a judge gives; tsedaqah is the rightness of the relationships that verdict protects. The king is asked to be given both by God: 'Endow the king' is a request that God place them in his hands. Verse 1 also names him 'the king' and 'the son of the king,' ben-melech, a double phrase that makes the psalm a prayer at the hinge of a dynasty.

In verse 3 the mountains and hills bring shalom, peace, and righteousness. Shalom is not the absence of war but wholeness, everything in its right place. The mountains, usually places of defence, are pictured here as channels of prosperity for the people. Solomon's own name is from the same root, which makes the wish about his reign a wish about his name.

Verse 4 sets two words for the poor beside a verb for their enemy. 'Afflicted' is ani, the same word as in Psalm 70:5; 'needy' is evyon; and the verse closes with dakka, to crush, used of what happens to the oppressor. The crushing that the poor usually suffer is turned onto the one who crushes. Verse 12 repeats the pairing 'needy who cry out' and 'afflicted who have no helper,' and verse 13 adds 'poor' and 'needy' again. The king answers the poor because he hears them cry.

In verse 5 the BSB text has 'May they fear him,' but a footnote records that the Septuagint reads 'He shall endure,' which fits the preceding lines about sun and moon. The Hebrew as it stands can also be read as addressed to God, 'may they fear You as long as the sun shines.' The difference shows how carefully a translator must weigh the text, and it does not change the psalm's point that the reign lasts.

In verse 8 the BSB footnote says the Hebrew has 'the River' where the translation supplies 'the Euphrates.' The phrase 'from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth' is the same one used in Zechariah 9:10. The land promise to Abraham in Genesis 15:18 also runs to the great River, the Euphrates. The psalm takes the boundary of the promise and stretches it to the ends of the earth.

In verse 9 the king's enemies 'lick the dust.' Micah 7:17 uses the same picture for the nations who 'will lick the dust like a snake,' and it recalls the curse on the serpent to go on its belly and eat dust, Genesis 3:14. The defeated are not just beaten; they take on the posture of the serpent.

Verse 14 says the king 'will redeem' the oppressed, using ga'al, the verb for the kinsman-redeemer who buys back a relative, and that their blood is 'precious,' yaqar, in his sight. The king takes the role of the family protector, a role Scripture elsewhere gives to God.

Verse 17's 'may all nations be blessed' has a footnote, 'Or increase.' The verb pattern is a reflexive one, the same shape as in Genesis 22:18 and 26:4, so the sense may be 'bless themselves by him,' that is, use his name as a pattern of blessing, or 'be blessed in him.' Either way the wording is drawn from the promise to Abraham.

typology.type: The king endowed with God's justice, verses 1 and 2
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 11:1 to 5 describes the shoot from Jesse's stump on whom the Spirit rests, who judges the poor with righteousness and decides with equity for the lowly. Jesus fulfils this: the Spirit descended on Him at His baptism, Luke 3:22, and He declared that He came to preach good news to the poor, Luke 4:18. Solomon received wisdom for judging as a gift and later lost the way; Christ is the King in whom justice is not given from outside but shown in Himself, and His judgment is perfect, John 5:30. The type falls short because Solomon's justice failed under the weight of his own heart.

typology.type: Dominion from sea to sea, verses 8 to 11
typology.fulfillment: The psalm's universal rule is taken up in Zechariah 9:9 and 10, where the king comes on a donkey and his dominion extends from sea to sea. Matthew applies the donkey text to Jesus at His entry into Jerusalem, Matthew 21:5. After the resurrection He says that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Him, Matthew 28:18, and in Revelation people from every tribe and tongue and nation are purchased by His blood, Revelation 5:9. The escalation is that His kingdom is spread through a gospel and not by armies. The type falls short since Solomon's empire was held by tribute and fear, and it broke on his death.

typology.type: The kings bringing gifts, verses 10 and 15
typology.fulfillment: Kings from Tarshish, Sheba and Seba bring tribute in the psalm. The magi come from the east and give the infant Jesus gold, frankincense and myrrh, Matthew 2:11, and Isaiah 60:6 sees the caravans of Sheba bringing gold and frankincense. Revelation completes the picture: 'the kings of the earth will bring their glory' into the city, Revelation 21:24. The correspondence begins in a house in Bethlehem and reaches its end in the new Jerusalem. The type falls short because Solomon received gifts as a rich king, while Christ receives them as the One who owns the world.

typology.type: The redeemer of the poor, verses 12 to 14
typology.fulfillment: The king redeems the needy from oppression and violence because their blood is precious to him. Jesus answers John the Baptist's question by pointing to the works that show He is the coming One, and the last of them is that 'the good news is preached to the poor,' Matthew 11:5. At the cross He redeems at the price of His own blood, 1 Peter 1:18 and 19. The psalm's king held the poor precious; Christ holds them so precious that He gave His life. The type falls short because Solomon's kingdom placed a heavy yoke on the poor, 1 Kings 12:4.

study.christ:
Psalm 72 leads to Christ by the shape of a King who cannot be fully matched by any earthly ruler. It asks for a reign that lasts as long as the sun, that reaches to the ends of the earth, that protects the poor and that becomes a blessing for every nation. Israel's history never produced such a king, and Israel knew it, because the same Psalter contains Psalm 89, where the promise appears to lie in ruins. The psalm therefore leaves a gap between what it asks and what history gave, and the New Testament claims that Jesus is the one who fills it.

The link by promise is explicit. Gabriel says of Jesus, 'The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David, and He will reign over the house of Jacob forever. His kingdom will never end,' Luke 1:32 and 33. This is Psalm 72:5, 7 and 17 in the form of an announcement. The prophets who stand between the psalm and the Gospels, especially Isaiah 9:6 and 7 and Isaiah 11:1 to 5, reshape the psalm's wishes into promises about a coming King from David's line, and the Gospels read Jesus as that King.

The link by contrast is sharp. Jesus Himself draws it when He says that the Queen of the South came to hear the wisdom of Solomon, 'and now One greater than Solomon is here,' Matthew 12:42. The psalm was prayed for a son who received the kings of the earth and then lost his heart to other gods, 1 Kings 11:4. Jesus receives the magi in a house, not a palace, and at the end refuses to use power to save Himself. The wisdom and justice that Solomon only reflected are found in Him without limit.

The link by theme is the poor. The heart of the psalm lies in verses 12 to 14: the king delivers the needy who cry out, takes pity on the weak, redeems them from oppression, and values their blood. The Gospels present exactly this King. Jesus announces good news to the poor, Luke 4:18, tells John's disciples that the poor have good news preached to them, Matthew 11:5, and calls 'blessed' the poor in spirit, Matthew 5:3. The redemption of blood in verse 14 becomes literal at the cross: He purchased people for God by His blood, Revelation 5:9.

The link by blessing to the nations is the psalm's climax. 'In him may all nations be blessed' picks up the promise to Abraham, and Paul insists that the promise was spoken to Abraham and to his offspring, meaning one person, who is Christ, Galatians 3:16. Peter tells the crowd in Jerusalem that God raised up His Servant to bless them, Acts 3:25 and 26. Jesus says, 'I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everyone to Myself,' John 12:32. The prayer for a blessed world is answered in the cross.

Finally, Revelation completes the picture: the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever, Revelation 11:15. The psalm's wishes that he rule 'as long as the sun shines' find their final form in a reign with no end.

A caution: not every detail is a code. The Tarshish ships and the grain on the hills are poetry of blessing, not disguised predictions. The New Testament's use of the psalm rests on its main lines: the King, the poor, the nations, and the endless reign.
study.god:
The psalm gives a picture of God as the source of all just rule. Its first line asks that God endow the king with His justice, which assumes that justice belongs to God first and can only be given to others. The king's judgments, the peace on the mountains, and the redemption of the poor are all reflections of a justice that God has and shares. This corrects the assumption that human authority is self-standing. The good ruler is one who has been given something by God, and the bad one is one who has lost hold of it.

It shows God's special concern for the poor. The king's most important work in the psalm is to rescue the needy, and this work is described in language borrowed from God's own dealings with Israel. The king 'redeems' them, the word for the kinsman who buys back his relatives, and he treats their blood as precious. The Bible elsewhere speaks of God as the defender of the fatherless, the widow and the poor, and the psalm assumes that anyone who reigns on His behalf will share His priorities. The test of a king is the test of God's own heart.

The psalm shows God's rule over the natural world. Rain on mown grass, grain on the hilltops, orchards like the forests of Lebanon, and cities like the grass of the field are pictured as the fruit of a just reign. The link between righteousness and fertility is deep in Scripture. God is the One who provides both justice and abundance, and a land where the poor are oppressed is out of joint with creation.

It shows God's faithfulness to His promise. The blessing of the nations in verse 17 is a deliberate echo of Abraham, and God's purpose to bless the whole world through one family is treated as something that has not been forgotten. The psalm, prayed at the moment of a royal succession, is a sign that God's plan does not depend on a single reign.

It shows God as the One who alone acts. The closing doxology says that the LORD 'alone does marvelous deeds,' verse 18. The prayer for a great king ends by saying that he is not great at all without God. Every good gift that the king brings comes from God, and every honor that the king receives finally belongs to Him. The wish that 'all the earth be filled with His glory,' verse 19, is the deepest aim of the psalm: not the greatness of the king but the fame of God.

For worship, the psalm teaches us to pray for those in authority in the terms God Himself has set, that they will rule with justice and defend the weak. It teaches us to view our own service and power in the light of the poor. And it invites us to lift our eyes to the King who fulfils the prayer and to end, as the psalm does, with 'Amen and amen.'

crossReferences.note: Solomon's own first request as king is for an understanding heart to judge God's people and discern good from evil. It reads like the answer to the opening of Psalm 72. It shows that the psalm's wish for a king with God's justice was one Solomon himself shared at the start of his reign.

The Queen of Sheba says God made Solomon king 'to carry out justice and righteousness.' The language is very close to Psalm 72:1. Her visit and gifts also correspond to verses 10 and 15, and Solomon's reign at its best therefore gives a picture of what the psalm asks.

After Solomon's death the people ask his son to lighten the heavy yoke his father put on them. The psalm's king was to relieve the oppressed, and this text shows the actual reign leaving many weighed down. The contrast sends the reader looking for a better King.

The shoot from Jesse's stump will judge the poor with righteousness and decide with equity for the lowly. The passage takes the central concerns of Psalm 72, justice for the poor and righteousness as the king's belt, and promises them for a coming Davidic ruler.

The humble king riding on a donkey will proclaim peace to the nations, and his dominion will run from sea to sea, and from the Euphrates to the ends of the earth. The last words nearly repeat Psalm 72:8, and Matthew applies the donkey text to Jesus.

God tells Abraham that through his offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed. Psalm 72:17 takes up this promise and applies it to the Davidic king, showing that Israel understood the throne as the means by which God would bless the world.

The covenant with David promises that his offspring will endure forever and his throne be like the sun and moon. The images are those of Psalm 72:5 and 17. Book III ends by asking where this promise has gone, so the two psalms bracket the story of the Davidic hope.

Jesus says the Queen of the South came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon's wisdom, and now One greater than Solomon is here. The saying takes Solomon's visitors from the psalm's picture and sets them beside Jesus, claiming for Him what the psalm asks for the king.

Gabriel promises Mary that her son will have David's throne and that His kingdom will never end. The announcement is Psalm 72's endless reign and Davidic kingship, spoken now as a promise about a particular person.

The seventh trumpet announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever. The verse is the final answer to the psalm's prayer that all kings bow down to him and all nations serve him.

In the new Jerusalem the nations walk by its light and the kings of the earth bring their glory into it. This is the fulfillment of the tribute of Psalm 72:10 and 11, given not to a conqueror but to the Lamb, and given freely by those who love him.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 72 sits at a crossing of the Bible's main lines. From creation the human race was given dominion over the earth, Genesis 1:26, meant to rule under God with care for the world and each other. The fall bent that rule into oppression, and the first great acts of violence in Genesis 4 are the strong destroying the weak. Kings in the ancient world took up the task badly. The psalm imagines the reign that human dominion was always meant to be: justice from God, peace in the land, the weak defended and the earth fruitful.

The promise to Abraham gives the psalm its aim. God told him that through his offspring all nations would be blessed, Genesis 22:18. The promise to David, 2 Samuel 7:12 to 16, narrowed it to a royal line whose throne would be established forever. Psalm 72 is the point where the two promises are joined in prayer. The son of David is asked to be the channel of Abraham's blessing. The mediation of blessing that seemed to belong to a whole people is placed on the shoulders of one king.

The history that follows shows how far the reality fell from the prayer. Solomon's reign began well and ended with a divided heart, Israel divided, and later kings did worse. The exile ended the line's rule. Psalm 89 at the end of Book III mourns that the crown is in the dust. The Psalter keeps the prayer of Psalm 72 alive through all of that, because it has become a hope rather than a report, and the prophets keep restating it in new forms: a shoot from Jesse, a righteous Branch, a king on a donkey.

The answer arrives in Jesus. He is the Son of David whose kingdom has no end, Luke 1:32 and 33. He defended the poor, took the oppressed into His care, redeemed them with His blood, and drew people from every nation to Himself. Paul can say that the offspring promised to Abraham is Christ, Galatians 3:16. After His resurrection He is enthroned at the right hand of God, Psalm 110:1 and Acts 2:34 to 36, and He rules now over those who confess Him, while the world waits for the day when every knee will bow.

The story ends in the new creation with the psalm fulfilled to the letter. The kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of Christ, Revelation 11:15. The kings of the earth bring their glory into the city, Revelation 21:24. The poor are no longer oppressed, since God wipes away every tear and there is no more death, mourning, crying or pain, Revelation 21:4. The glory of God fills the earth, and the psalm's last prayer, 'may all the earth be filled with His glory. Amen and amen,' is answered by a whole creation saying the same.

quiz.q: What does the psalmist ask God to give the king, verse 1?

options.text: God's own justice and righteousness.
options.note: The king's fitness to rule is asked to come directly from God's character, not human wisdom alone.

options.text: Great wealth and many horses.
options.note: The prayer centers on justice and righteousness, not material accumulation.

options.text: A large standing army.
options.note: The psalm never asks for military strength as the foundation of the reign.

options.text: Freedom from all responsibility.
options.note: The opposite; the king is asked to take up the weighty responsibility of just rule.

quiz.q: How far does the psalm envision this king's rule extending, verse 8?

options.text: From sea to sea and from the Euphrates to the ends of the earth.
options.note: This universal scope exceeds any historical king's actual territory.

options.text: Only within the city of Jerusalem.
options.note: The psalm's vision is explicitly universal, not merely local.

options.text: Only over the twelve tribes of Israel.
options.note: The vision goes beyond Israel to all nations and kings of the earth.

options.text: Only as far as neighboring Egypt.
options.note: The psalm names the Euphrates and 'the ends of the earth,' far exceeding Egypt alone.

quiz.q: What does the king do for the needy and afflicted, verses 12-14?

options.text: He delivers, takes pity on, and redeems them from oppression and violence, valuing their blood as precious.
options.note: This compassionate rescue is central to the psalm's picture of true kingship.

options.text: He taxes them further to fund his court.
options.note: The opposite; he defends and rescues the poor rather than burdening them.

options.text: He ignores them in favor of the wealthy.
options.note: The psalm specifically highlights his care for those who have no helper.

options.text: He exiles them from the land.
options.note: The text describes rescue and redemption, not exile.

quiz.q: What does verse 17 promise will happen to all nations in this king?

options.text: All nations will be blessed in him, echoing God's promise to Abraham.
options.note: This deliberately recalls Genesis 12:3, tying the psalm to God's covenant purpose for the whole world.

options.text: All nations will be destroyed by him.
options.note: The psalm envisions blessing, not destruction, extending to the nations.

options.text: All nations will forget his name.
options.note: The opposite; his name is promised to endure forever, verse 17.

options.text: All nations will be forced into slavery.
options.note: The psalm describes willing blessing and homage, not forced slavery.

quiz.q: What note closes this psalm and Book II of the Psalter, verse 20?

options.text: "Thus conclude the prayers of David son of Jesse."
options.note: This marks a deliberate structural close to the collection of David's prayers at this point in the Psalter.

options.text: A call to build a new temple.
options.note: No such call appears; the psalm closes in doxology and this concluding note.

options.text: A warning against future kings.
options.note: The psalm closes in blessing and praise, not warning.

options.text: A genealogy of Solomon's descendants.
options.note: No genealogy appears; the psalm ends with worship and this closing note.

questions: This psalm prays that the king would receive God's own justice and righteousness, not merely human wisdom, verse 1. Where in your own responsibilities do you need to ask God for His justice rather than trusting your own judgment?
The ideal king rescues the needy who have no helper, verses 12-14. Who around you has no helper, and what would it look like to reflect the compassion of the true King toward them?

This psalm's vision, universal peace, an everlasting name, blessing to all nations, was always too large for Solomon. Where do you see this hope beginning to be fulfilled in Christ's kingdom today, and where are you still waiting for it in full?

Verse 17 ties this king's reign to God's ancient promise that all nations would be blessed through Abraham's offspring. How does knowing you are part of that blessed multitude in Christ shape your sense of belonging to God's people?

The psalm closes by noting that David's prayers are concluded, yet the hope it expresses continues through the rest of Scripture. What unfulfilled hope in your own life do you need to entrust to God's larger, unfolding purposes?

translationNotes.note: Some ancient manuscripts, reflected in a few translations, read 'He shall endure as long as the sun,' rather than 'may they fear him,' a small variant that does not change the psalm's overall hope for an enduring, reverenced reign.
'The Euphrates' renders a Hebrew phrase literally meaning 'the River,' the standard way the Euphrates is designated in the Old Testament as the far boundary of the promised land, Genesis 15:18.
'May his name continue' can also be rendered 'may his name increase,' both readings pointing to an ever-growing, never-fading reputation for this king, in contrast to every merely human ruler's fame.
